Classification guard: the single edge asserts association only (etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, hypothesizedOnly:true, mechanismCategory PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL) as a case-matching presentation-and-workup edge on the genitofemoral-nerve-neuralgia and glomus-tumor precedent. The chronic anorectal pain is largely constitutive of the syndrome - Rome IV defines chronic proctalgia (levator ani syndrome) as recurrent or continuous rectal pain lasting more than 30 minutes with puborectalis tenderness on digital rectal examination - so the edge records that this presentation enters the exclusionary chronic-pain workup rather than asserting a distinct downstream pain disorder. Individual claims require documented levator ani syndrome by Rome criteria with puborectalis tenderness, a dated exclusionary anorectal and pelvic workup, and review by a qualified medical professional.

Pathway and duplicate-scope screens: no edge to anismus-pelvic-floor-dyssynergia (the Rome IV taxonomy separates the pain syndrome from the defecation disorder; paradoxical contraction co-prevalence is comorbidity, and anismus is a sibling identity that authors its own windows); no edge to fecal-incontinence (the published anismus-pelvic-floor-dyssynergia -> fecal-incontinence window already carries the pelvic-floor outlet pathway, and the located soiling and postprandial-defecation cohorts are functional-GI-overlap class without levator-ani-specific outcome direction, PMID 29987361 and PMID 27824643); no edge to chronic-pelvic-pain-syndrome (constitutive - the Chiarioni systematic review treats chronic proctalgia as one of the chronic pelvic pain syndromes, so an edge would restate the diagnostic family); no edge to irritable-bowel-syndrome (the Rome-III overlap clustering of 2819 functional-GI outpatients found levator ani syndrome a homogeneous single-disorder group rather than an overlap driver, PMID 33555092 - negative overlap evidence); no edge to depressive-disorder despite documented association (see governance notes for the reopening condition).
governanceNotes: D1 batch 53 (2026-09-25): one bounded association edge authored - levator ani syndrome to unexplained-chronic-pain (rank 1) - classified ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, and hypothesizedOnly:true; mechanismCategory PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL. The proposition rests on the Bharucha and Lee 2016 Mayo Clinic Proceedings review of anorectal and pelvic pain, which places levator ani syndrome among the chronic pelvic pain conditions that share associations with dysfunctional voiding or defecation, comorbid conditions including fibromyalgia and depression, impaired quality of life, and increased health care utilization, and implicates pelvic floor muscle tension, peripheral inflammation, peripheral and central sensitization, and psychosocial factors in pathogenesis with multidisciplinary management (PMID 27712641), on the Knowles and Cohen 2022 Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine review organizing chronic anal pain into local causes, functional anorectal pain (proctalgia fugax, levator ani syndrome), and neuropathic pain syndromes (pudendal neuralgia, coccygodynia) with the diagnostic tests and treatments that distinguish them (PMID 35649568), and on the Chiarioni 2011 World Journal of Gastroenterology systematic review documenting that chronic or recurrent pain of the anal canal, rectum, and other pelvic organs affects 7 to 24 percent of the population with impaired quality of life and high health care costs, that excessive tension in the striated pelvic-floor muscles appears common to most of the pelvic pain syndromes, and that biofeedback selected by levator tenderness achieved 85 percent success in a randomized chronic-proctalgia trial (PMID 22110274). The literature documents a reproducible chronic idiopathic anorectal pain presentation whose exclusionary workup mirrors the unexplained-chronic-pain evaluation without establishing that levator ani syndrome produced a distinct chronic pain disorder in any individual.

Counter-evidence and caveat screens recorded 2026-09-25: (i) constitutive-pain guard - the pain defines the syndrome, so the edge is presentation-and-workup matching rather than a causal arrow, following the genitofemoral-nerve-neuralgia and glomus-tumor case-matching edges; (ii) taxonomy permeability - Rome IV subdivides functional anorectal pain by duration and examination findings only, and chronic proctalgia is thought secondary to paradoxical pelvic floor contraction in many patients, so levator ani syndrome overlaps mechanistically with dyssynergic defecation and pudendal neuropathy; (iii) evidence class - the anchors are systematic-review and specialty-review class with one randomized treatment trial, not incidence or natural-history cohorts; (iv) bidirectional attribution - central sensitization and psychosocial factors may produce both the pain and the health care utilization recorded in the anchors.

Negative screens recorded 2026-09-25: (i) no levator-ani-syndrome-to-depressive-disorder edge - depression is documented as a comorbid condition at review level (PMID 27712641) and clinical depression was present in five of ten chronic idiopathic anal pain patients in a sacral-nerve-stimulation pilot (PMID 23692279) with psychological burden described qualitatively (PMID 32519087), but no levator-ani-syndrome-specific quantified depression cohort was located; reopening condition: a condition-specific cohort or case-control quantifying depressive-disorder prevalence in Rome-defined levator ani syndrome; (ii) no -> anismus-pelvic-floor-dyssynergia, -> fecal-incontinence, -> chronic-pelvic-pain-syndrome, or -> irritable-bowel-syndrome edge (see todo screens; the anismus identity owns the outlet-incontinence pathway and the overlap-clustering evidence is negative for levator ani syndrome as an overlap driver); (iii) no -> hemorrhoids, -> anal-fissure, or -> pruritus-ani edge (local anorectal causes are alternative diagnoses to exclude in the workup rather than downstream conditions, per the Knowles review categories).

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The Bharucha and Lee 2016 Mayo Clinic Proceedings review documents that chronic anorectal and pelvic pain conditions including levator ani syndrome share associations with dysfunctional voiding or defecation, comorbid conditions such as fibromyalgia and depression, impaired quality of life, and increased health care utilization, with pelvic floor muscle tension, peripheral inflammation, peripheral and central sensitization, and psychosocial factors implicated in pathogenesis and multidisciplinary management recommended (PMID 27712641); the Knowles and Cohen 2022 review organizes chronic anal pain into local causes, functional anorectal pain including levator ani syndrome, and neuropathic pain syndromes such as pudendal neuralgia and coccygodynia, describing the diagnostic tests and treatments that separate them (PMID 35649568); the Chiarioni 2011 systematic review documents that chronic or recurrent anorectal and pelvic pain affects 7 to 24 percent of the population with impaired quality of life, that excessive striated-muscle tension of the pelvic floor is common to most pelvic pain syndromes, and that a randomized trial achieved 85 percent success with biofeedback in chronic proctalgia selected by levator tenderness (PMID 22110274); the literature documents a reproducible severe chronic idiopathic anorectal pain presentation requiring an exclusionary local, functional, and neuropathic workup without establishing that levator ani syndrome caused a distinct chronic pain disorder in any individual.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: The mapping does not assert that levator ani syndrome caused an individual's chronic pain disorder: the pain lasting more than 30 minutes with puborectalis tenderness is the defining diagnostic presentation of the syndrome rather than a separate downstream condition, so the edge records presentation-and-workup matching; the anchor literature is systematic- and specialty-review class with one randomized treatment trial rather than incidence cohorts, central sensitization and psychosocial factors may drive both the pain and the documented health care utilization, and pudendal neuralgia, coccygodynia, local anorectal disease, urologic chronic pelvic pain, and referred spine or sacroiliac pain are competing explanations of the same presentation - so no directional claim is made.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized spasm-sensitization route is described: paradoxical contraction and sustained tension of the puborectalis and pelvic-floor striated muscles is thought to produce local ischemic and mechanical strain that sustains the anorectal pain, while peripheral inflammation, peripheral and central sensitization, and psychosocial factors amplify and maintain the pain state; the located reviews document levator tenderness as the selecting physical sign for biofeedback response and pelvic floor tension among the implicated pathogenic factors, but the individual contributions of spasm, sensitization, and psychosocial overlay remain hypotheses rather than quantified pathways.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. The chronic anorectal pain of levator ani syndrome is documented in specialty and systematic reviews as a disabling presentation sharing sensitization and psychosocial features with the chronic pelvic pain family, and its exclusionary workup is the same evaluation applied to unexplained chronic pain, but individual determination requires Rome-criteria documentation of levator ani syndrome with puborectalis tenderness, a dated anorectal examination, anorectal manometry or balloon expulsion testing where performed, pelvic floor assessment, exclusion of local anorectal and neuropathic causes, and review by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Documentation of the levator ani syndrome diagnosis (Rome IV criteria: recurrent or continuous rectal pain lasting more than 30 minutes, with tenderness of the levator ani muscle on digital rectal examination) with the date of diagnosis and the examining clinician; anorectal physiology testing where performed (anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion test, defecography or magnetic resonance defecography) and pelvic floor physiotherapy or biofeedback records with response; documentation of pain severity, location, duration, and aggravating or relieving factors with chronology; the exclusionary workup for local causes (hemorrhoids, anal fissure, abscess, fistula, rectal prolapse, solitary rectal ulcer, neoplasm, proctitis, inflammatory bowel disease) and for neuropathic and referred causes (pudendal neuralgia, coccygodynia, sacroiliac or lumbar spine disease, urologic chronic pelvic pain, prostatitis, interstitial cystitis, vulvodynia); records of comorbid functional pain conditions (fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, chronic fatigue) and psychological screening with dates; colorectal, pain-medicine, or pelvic-floor-medicine assessment of the chronic pain attribution
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Pudendal neuralgia or other anorectal neuropathic pain syndromes
Coccygodynia and sacroiliac or lumbar spine referred pain
Local anorectal disease (hemorrhoids, anal fissure, abscess, fistula, rectal prolapse, solitary rectal ulcer, neoplasm, inflammatory bowel disease)
Urologic chronic pelvic pain (chronic prostatitis, interstitial cystitis) or vulvodynia
Dyssynergic defecation or inadequate defecatory propulsion as the primary defecation disorder
Central sensitization, mood, or psychosocial amplification of the pain state

suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY as a case-matching pain edge on the genitofemoral-nerve-neuralgia and glomus-tumor precedent: specialty and systematic reviews document a chronic idiopathic anorectal pain syndrome defined by pain duration and puborectalis tenderness whose exclusionary local, functional, and neuropathic workup mirrors the unexplained-chronic-pain evaluation, with pelvic floor striated-muscle tension and central sensitization as implicated factors; because the pain is constitutive of the syndrome, the evidence class is review-level, and competing neuropathic and local explanations are enumerated in the same reviews, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only and records presentation-and-workup matching rather than a causal arrow.
